claims.text: The equatorial climate, found within about ten degrees of the Equator, is hot all year, with average temperatures close to 26-28 degrees Celsius in every month, and wet, usually receiving over 2000 mm of rain a year with no dry season, because the midday sun stays high throughout the year.

claims.text: In an equatorial climate the sun heats the ground strongly each day, so air rises, cools and condenses into tall storm clouds, which gives heavy convectional rainfall most afternoons: sunny mornings and stormy afternoons are the daily pattern.

claims.text: The hot desert climate has a large daily and annual temperature range, very hot afternoons and cool nights, and less than 250 mm of rain a year, often far less; hot deserts are dry because air sinks in high-pressure belts and brings no clouds, because cold ocean currents cool and dry the air above them, and because some deserts lie too far from the sea for moist winds to reach them.

claims.text: On a climate graph, rainfall is shown by bars read in millimetres and temperature by a line read in degrees Celsius; the daily (diurnal) temperature range is the difference between the highest and lowest temperature in one day, while the annual temperature range is the difference between the warmest and the coldest month.

claims.text: An ecosystem is all the plants and animals of an area together with the soil, water and climate they depend on; a tropical rainforest grows in layers from emergent trees through a dense canopy to a shaded floor, its nutrients cycle quickly because dead leaves rot fast, and a single hectare can hold more than two hundred tree species.

claims.text: Rainforest plant adaptations compete for light rather than store water: drip tips channel heavy rain off the pointed leaf so it dries, buttress roots hold tall trees upright in the shallow soil, and lianas climb the trunks to reach the canopy light.

claims.text: Desert plants survive scarce water by storing it in fat succulent stems, cutting water loss with spines or small leaves, or spreading long or shallow roots to catch brief showers; desert animals such as the oryx mostly graze at dawn and dusk or come out at night, as the fog-drinking welwitschia of the Namib shows on the plant side.

claims.text: Deforestation is the large-scale clearing of forest; tropical rainforest is cleared for commercial logging, cattle ranching, shifting and commercial crop farming (including soya and oil palm, whose fruit yields palm oil, a vegetable oil, not a mineral oil from the ground), mining, and for dams and roads.

claims.text: Removing trees causes local effects near the cleared area: rain that leaves no longer intercept washes away the exposed soil, run-off reaches rivers faster so flooding downstream grows worse, and the plants and animals of the habitat are lost.

claims.text: Deforestation also has global effects, which reach the whole planet rather than the cleared area: burning and rotting vegetation releases carbon dioxide, which adds to the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming, and species lost with the forest reduce the world's biodiversity.
